Friday 9/18/2026 p.m.
Stocks mixed following yesterday's gains
- The Nasdaq finished higher, led by semiconductor stocks, while the Dow ended slightly lower following the post-Fed rally. Oil prices fell for the third consecutive day, but that didn’t stop bond yields from rising. On the macroeconomic front, the biggest development was the Bank of Japan's decision to raise interest rates by a quarter point to 1.25%, as expected, marking the highest policy rate since 1995. However, the yen weakened against the U.S. dollar as the vote included two dissents, fueling some skepticism about the pace of future policy tightening. The S&P 500 was little changed for the week, as strength in communication services, healthcare, and technology stocks was offset by weakness in the utilities and financials sectors.
Long-term yields little changed after Fed hike
- After a busy week for central banks, bond prices stabilized somewhat this week, though with yields remaining near multi-year highs. The Fed hiked interest rates this month for the first time since 2023, and officials are pointing to one more hike before the end of the year. With consumer spending resilient, the AI buildout continuing, and the labor market solid, the Fed was running out of reasons to stay on the sidelines after more than five years of above-target inflation. While the latest move by the Fed isn't likely one-and-done, it also doesn't look to us like the start of an aggressive rate-hiking cycle. In our view, the Fed isn't as far behind the curve as it was in 2022. A mid-cycle adjustment that potentially unwinds the rate cuts delivered last year, while leaving the 2024 cuts in place, is our base case. We believe equities responded positively and long-term bond yields declined following the hike because the move reinforced the Fed's inflation-fighting credibility and independence. As a result, long-term market-based inflation expectations eased and remain consistent with the Fed achieving its inflation target over time.
Oil prices and geopolitics in focus next week
– Despite today's divergence, the positive relationship between oil prices and bond yields has strengthened to its highest level since 2020, as ongoing tensions in the Middle East have become a key driver of inflation this year. As a result, developments in energy markets will remain important for both central bank policy and global trade. Looking ahead to next week, the main event will be the September 24 meeting between President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, marking Xi's first trip to the United States since 2023. Expectations are that the meeting will lead to an extension of the U.S.-China trade truce, which is currently set to expire in November. Trump is also expected to meet with Gulf state leaders to discuss the conflict involving Iran. On the economic calendar, it will be a relatively quiet week, with the preliminary U.S. Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) scheduled for release on Wednesday.
Angelo Kourkafas, CFA

Happy Thursday. Breaking news this morning: Nvidia has agreed to buy open-source artificial intelligence platform Hugging Face
for nearly $13 billion.
Stock futures
are mixed this morning after a
winning day
on Wall Street.
Here are five key things investors need to know to start the trading day:
1. Summit up
The G20 wrapped up its two-day Innovation Ministerial yesterday, where technology leaders and government representatives talked artificial intelligence, data centers and tariffs.
Here are some of the biggest headlines out of the gathering:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said that AI will “democratize intelligence” for G20 countries and called the technology “the great equalizer.”
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, meanwhile, said using AI is a “non-negotiable” for countries, comparing the adoption of AI to the adoption of electricity.
Palantir CEO Alex Karp acknowledged that there are “huge dangers” to the technology but pushed back on what he called the “doom message” around AI. He appeared to allude to Anthropic and its CEO, who have warned about the technology’s risks.
On the data center front, Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown said he “really loved” President Donald Trump’s Monday Truth Social post, in which the president said communities who opposed data centers “want to end up being backwards and poor.”
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said that data centers will “bring prosperity” and are “getting a bad rap.” He also downplayed the facilities’ water consumption.
Catch up on all the biggest moments here.
2. Bond, John Bond
After hitting its
highest level since 2023
, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield pulled back in Wednesday’s session, providing relief for other corners of the market.
New York Federal Reserve President John Williams told CNBC yesterday that the recent yield jumps should be seen as
a sign of a strong economy
rather than as market dysfunction. Williams also said he would have to “wait and see” before deciding whether an interest rate hike would be necessary to calm inflation.
The three major averages snapped three-day losing streaks yesterday.
Follow live market updates here.
3. Snow forecast
Snowflake soared 24%
